newsitem.title: USA: Motorola not seen improving soon - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Motorola not seen improving soon - analysts.

text.p: Motorola Inc, having reported significantly lower third-quarter earnings, is not expected to show a substantial improvement in the fourth quarter.

"The key thing is not to expect much of an uptick in '97, at least in the near term....Things will probably be worse in the fourth quarter overall before they start to get modestly better," Hambrecht & Quist analyst Rakesh Sood said on Monday. "They came so close to losing money in semiconductors."

Motorola's third-quarter earnings fell to $0.34 a share from $0.81 in the same period last year, largely in line with analysts' most recent forecasts. Its net margin on sales dropped to 3.2 percent from 7.2 percent in the 1995 third quarter.

In September, the company cautioned that earnings would fall significantly short of initial expectations because of continued weakness in the semiconductor and cellular phone handset markets, especially in markets outside the United States.
Its third-quarter sales in the semiconductor segment fell 19 percent to $1.8 billion, and orders dropped 33 percent.
On Monday, Motorola said it expected a modest improvement in the semiconductor business in 1997.
"There is a notorious inability to forecast in the semiconductor industry," said Robert Wilkes, an analyst for Brown Brothers Harriman. "I think it makes sense to not be too optimistic."
Analysts said they were expecting to gain additional information about Motorola's cost-cutting efforts when the company held a conference call early Tuesday.

In a release, Motorola said it was taking actions to reduce operating expenses while deferring capital expenditures. It said it expected capital spending of about $3.1 billion in 1996, down from $4.2 billion.
The company said it would expand its cost-cutting efforts, including "work force adjustments," which will hold back fourth-quarter earnings.

"The expense controls is something that is going to be taken much more seriously," Sood said. "The gross margins have come down fairly dramatically, and one of the ways to offset that -- since they can't seem to do much given the market conditions -- is with manufacturing and workforce adjustments."

To be sure, analysts identified a few bright spots, such a strong cellular infrastructure and two-way paging orders. In addition, they said new cellular phone handsets, such as those based on CDMA (code division multiple access) technology, would give Motorola a boost over its competitors and would carry higher prices.
"That would be viewed as potential bright spot but again later on in '97 rather than earlier," Sood said.
